result.reason: The passage is Abaye's objection to Rava based on the baraita interpreting 'im kesev,' which is precisely what the 'Im Kesev Question' section's prose describes.

The passage contains exactly Abaye's heichi dami question, the peshita objection, and the lama li kra argument leading to the non-obvious scenario — precisely what the 'Non-Obvious Case' prose describes.

The passage directly presents the Gemara's 'no, actually' response explaining the case as post-slaughter substitution and identifying the verse as a mere asmachta, which is exactly what heading 0's prose describes.
The passage directly states that the word 'lamb' (kesev) comes to include the Paschal lamb in the fat tail (alyah) requirement, which is precisely what the 'Fat Tail Law' section's prose discusses.

The passage explicitly teaches that a Paschal lamb whose year has passed and peace-offerings from a Paschal lamb require smicha, nesachim, and waving of breast and thigh — exactly the shelamim laws discussed in candidate 1's prose.
The passage directly discusses how 've-im ez' interrupts the matter to teach that a she-goat does not require the fat tail, which is exactly what the 'Goat Exclusion' prose section addresses.

Item 1 introduces the 'some teach this dispute with regard to the first clause' version, and items 2-5 present Rava's ruling in that version, Abaye's objection, and the refutation — all of which the prose under 'Temurah Timing' (index 0) explicitly describes as the reversed formulation where Rava's statement applies when the original was found before shechita and the temurah act was also before shechita, matching the content of all five items.

The passage contains exactly Shmuel's principle comparing chatas to pesach and Rabbi Yochanan's qualification about finding the animal after shechita, which is precisely what the 'Chatas Parallel' section's prose introduces and discusses.

Both items together constitute Rav Yosef's challenge to Shmuel: Item 1 is Rav Yosef invoking Reish Lakish's ruling about chatas she-avar shnaso going to graze, and Item 2 is the baraita showing that a pesach she-avra shnaso is brought as a shelamim — together forming the complete objection that the 'Reish Lakish View' prose describes.

The passage explicitly states Shmuel's principle applies only to 'avudim' (lost animals) and not 'dchuyim' (deferred/pushed aside), which is precisely what the 'Limited Scope' section's prose describes as the Gemara's answer narrowing Shmuel's principle to lost animal cases only.

The passage quotes the full mishna/braitta presenting both Rabbi's and the Rabbis' views as a single unit, and it is introduced as the Gemara's challenge regarding 'lost' sacrifices — this is the foundational text that the 'Rabbi's View' section explicitly describes as examining, making it the natural home for the complete quoted source before the essay separates out the two positions.

The entire passage builds toward and explicitly establishes that chatzot (not shechita) is the determinative moment for Shmuel — items 7, 9, and 10 all explicitly conclude 'chatzot kava' — which is precisely what the 'Chatzot Determines' section prose describes as the Gemara's core articulation.
